extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, reformers, and informed readers interested in American party politics and municipal reform
extracted.subtask_description: Tactics, legal remedies, and organizational guidance for combating political machines and boss rule in American cities; covers methods of attack (primaries, independent tickets, bolting, third parties), legislative regulation, and the social obstacles to reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack the primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The first form is an attack upon the primaries. They are the key of a Ring's position, and when they have been captured their batteries can be turned against the Ring itself. When an assault upon the bosses is resolved upon, the first thing is to form a committee. It issues a manifesto calling on all good citizens to attend the primaries of their respective wards, and there vote for delegates opposed to the Ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical obstacles: primary rolls are often prepared by professionals and exclude many voters (sometimes only one-fourth or one-fifth of voters are on the roll), so even patriotic turnout may be outvoted. The respectable and wealthy are apathetic or unwilling to endure rough primary surroundings. Success usually requires active organizing by a group of energetic young men to beat up the ward membership and 'beard' local bosses. Even when some primaries are won, conventions may still be controlled by professionals who manipulate delegates and chairmanships; historically this method rarely succeeds unless repeated and technically well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run an independent list (separate candidates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an independent list of nominations and run a separate set of candidates. If this strategy be resolved on, the primaries are left unheeded; but when the election approaches, a committee is formed which issues a list of candidates for some or all of the vacant offices in opposition to the 'regular' list issued by the party convention, and conducts the agitation on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saves trouble in primaries and conventions but requires organization of a complete campaign corps and raising a campaign fund. Average voters tend to adhere to party habits and vote the 'regular ticket,' so bolting independents rarely carry enough of their party to win; the result often lets in the opposing party's candidates. Expense and labor are heavy; risk of being 'sold out' historically was high (though some risks reduced by official voting papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scratching (abstaining from voting for specific ticket names)
rubrics_metrics.description: A third plan is to abstain from voting for the names on your party ticket to which you object. This is Scratching. You are spared the trouble of running candidates of your own, but your abstention, if the parties are nearly balanced, causes the defeat of the bad candidates whom your own party puts forward, and brings in those of the other party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to frighten a Ring or to defeat a few corrupt or dangerous men on an otherwise acceptable ticket. It avoids the expense of running independents but may cause the election of the opposite party if widely practiced; best used selectively when only certain names are objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vote the opposite party or coordinate with the opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If indignation against a dominant Ring has risen so high as to overcome party predilections, reformers will urge their friends to vote the ticket of the opposite party, either entire or at least all the better names on it, thus ensuring its victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient but 'desperate' because it may put another Ring in power; the goal is often punitive—to raise political standards by punishing evil doers. Preferable when reformers first make overtures to the opposite party and induce them, by the promise of support, to nominate better candidates (a non-partisan ticket). This scheme needs tact and sufficient numbers; the opposite party may refuse help or fear the consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a third party / Citizens' Ticket
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming a third party out of the best men of both regular organizations and starting a third set of candidates (a 'Citizens' Ticket').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extension and improvement of running independents because it draws votes from both parties rather than one only, giving it greater promise of success. Frequently employed in recently reformed or second-order cities; still expensive and organizationally demanding but can be successful when it unites the best from both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative remedies and regulation of primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a few States extended the penalties attached to bribery and frauds at public elections to similar offences committed at primaries and nominating conventions, deeming these acts scarcely less hurtful when practised at purely voluntary and private gatherings than when employed at elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Minnesota statutes (1887) made annulment or destruction of ballots at party meetings, wrongful prevention of persons entitled to vote, personation, or any other fraud tending to affect the result punishable by fine up to $3000, or three years' imprisonment, or both. Such laws protect delegates and candidates from fraud and were adopted because Machines had nullified voter freedom; critics (especially Europeans then) were surprised that government should regulate internal party proceedings, but the book argues it is justified to safeguard voluntary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize active volunteers to capture primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The best chance of capturing a primary is by the action of a group of active young men who will take the trouble of organizing the movement by beating up the members of the party who reside in the district, and bearding the local bosses in the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rough and toilsome piece of work, but young men find compensation in the fun and credit of victory. Respectable voters are often unwilling or unable to do such disagreeable work due to business, social discomfort, or aversion to rough crowds; therefore reform movements must rely on energetic organizers to mobilize local support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist with multiple remedies: social, educational, and legal
rubrics_metrics.description: If reformers attack the enemy at every point, using every social and educational as well as legal appliance, the example of their disinterested public spirit, and the cogency of their arguments, cannot fail to tell on the voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The struggle is a long war of volunteers against disciplined party professionals; victory depends on constancy, earnestness, not relying too absolutely on any one remedy, and sustained action over a series of elections. Legislative remedies help but internal causes (ignorance, apathy) require patient, unremitting diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the structural importance of primary composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of the primaries determines that of the local conventions, and the composition of the local conventions determines that of the national. To every delegate there is added an alternate chosen by the local convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because delegates to higher-level bodies come from primaries, control of primaries is the fundamental lever for influencing State and national nominations; reformers must therefore focus on the primary level to change party outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address voter apathy and ignorance among city electorates
rubrics_metrics.description: In great cities a large section of the voters will, for many years to come, be comparatively ignorant of the methods of free government which they are set to work. They will be ignorant even of their own interests, failing to perceive that wasteful expenditure injures those who do not pay direct taxes, as well as those who do. Once they have joined a party, they will vote at the bidding of its local leaders, however personally unworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This persistent social condition supplies material for rings and bosses; reform requires educational work, better leadership from the propertied classes, and the steady mobilization of 'better citizens.' Expect slow, generational progress; do not expect rapid elimination of Machine influence without widespread civic education and leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand varieties and prevalence of corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Bribery exists in Congress but is confined to a few members (about five per cent); taking other considerations than money (a share in a contract, a railway pass, a 'good thing' for a friend) prevails among legislators to a larger extent (roughly 15–20% of members may allow this). Malversation of public funds occurs occasionally in cities; jobbery (misuse of public position for individuals) is not rare and is common in large cities; patronage is usually dispensed to win party considerations or personal support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These empirical assessments indicate where to target reform: city governments and legislatures have higher incidence of jobbery and patronage than higher Federal officials or judges. Recognize differences between offices and jurisdictions when choosing remedies and measuring success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage is amplified by frequent removals and short terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Patronage is usually dispensed with a view to party considerations or to win personal support. The chief difference between the United States and places like England and France is that owing to the short terms and frequent removals the quantity of patronage is relatively greater in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural features of the political system (term length, turnover) affect the scale of patronage and thus the difficulty of reform; long-term institutional changes (civil service reform, reconstruction of city government) are among the legislative remedies recommended.
